title: Spotting misinformation online
examples: When I see something shocking online, what is the first thing I should do?
What is the difference between misinformation and disinformation?
Can you show me how to check if a picture is real?

explain.say: Today we are learning to spot misinformation online.

items: Think critically about what you read.
Don't share things without checking them first.
We will learn three key checking skills today.

explain.say: First, you must always check the source of the information.
Next, try lateral reading when you find a claim online.

items: Check what other reliable sources say

explain.say: Remember to check images for context when you see them.
For example, if you see a photo of a protest, check when and where it was taken.
In real life, if a friend sends you a strange warning about a local event, check the official council website.

faq.q: How do I know if a website is trustworthy?
faq.a: Look for professional news organizations or educational institutions. They usually have clear contact details and multiple sources citing their information. You could also ask a teacher or parent, or check if the site has a clear 'About Us' section.

faq.q: What is the difference between misinformation and disinformation?
faq.a: Misinformation is false information shared without knowing it is false. Disinformation is false information shared on purpose to mislead people. It is important to know the difference.
asks: What is the difference between mistake and lie online?

faq.q: If I see a shocking photo, what should I do first?
faq.a: Do not share it right away. First, try to find the original source of the image using a reverse image search tool. This can help you find out where and when it was first published. You could also ask a librarian or a knowledgeable adult.
asks: How do I check a picture?
Can I trust a photo from social media?

faq.a: It means you leave the original questionable page and open new tabs to see what other trusted sources say about the same topic. You are checking the claim from multiple angles. You could try searching the main claim on Google, or ask a friend to check sources with you.

faq.q: What if the source seems legitimate but the information is wrong?
faq.a: Even big sources can make mistakes. Always cross-reference the key facts with at least two other independent, reputable sources. Don't rely on just one place for important information. You could compare it to a textbook, or ask a subject teacher.
asks: Can big news sites be wrong?
How many sources should I check?

facts: Reputable sources usually cite their evidence and sources.
Lateral reading means checking a claim using multiple, different websites.
Images can be easily edited or taken out of their original time and place.
Always check the 'About Us' section of a website.

quiz.say: You see a headline claiming a major scientific discovery, but the website looks unprofessional and has many spelling errors. What is the best first step?

options.show: Look only at the picture to see if it looks real.
options.say: Look only at the picture to see if it looks real.

options.show: Check the website's URL and 'About Us' page for professionalism.
options.say: Check the website's URL and 'About Us' page for professionalism.

options.show: Immediately share it to warn others.
options.say: Immediately share it to warn others.

options.show: Search for the keywords on a different search engine.
options.say: Search for the keywords on a different search engine.

quiz.why: The source is the most important starting point; if the site looks unprofessional, the information is suspect.

wrong.0: Pictures can be easily manipulated or taken from different times.
wrong.2: Sharing it spreads the potential misinformation even if you are trying to help.
wrong.3: This only finds more potentially unreliable sources, not necessarily the truth.

quiz.say: A friend sends you a picture supposedly showing a rare animal in a specific location. What is the best way to verify the picture?

options.show: Use a reverse image search tool to find the original context.
options.say: Use a reverse image search tool to find the original context.

options.show: Ask the friend who sent it if they know the source.
options.say: Ask the friend who sent it if they know the source.

options.show: Assume it is true because the animal looks real.
options.say: Assume it is true because the animal looks real.

options.show: Just Google the animal's name to find more info.
options.say: Just Google the animal's name to find more info.

quiz.why: A reverse image search will show you where else that picture has appeared online, helping you find its original context.

wrong.1: The friend might also be misinformed or might not know the true origin.
wrong.2: The animal could be a different species or the photo could be old.
wrong.3: This only searches text and might not help you verify the picture itself.

quiz.say: You read a claim about history on a website. You check Wikipedia, and then you check two major university history department sites. Which method is best?

options.show: Checking multiple, independent, and reputable academic sources.
options.say: Checking multiple, independent, and reputable academic sources.

options.show: Checking only the most popular news site.
options.say: Checking only the most popular news site.

options.show: Asking a random person on a forum.
options.say: Asking a random person on a forum.

quiz.why: Relying on multiple, different, and trustworthy sources is the strongest way to confirm a historical fact.

wrong.1: Wikipedia is a good summary, but it should be backed up by primary academic sources.
wrong.2: Popularity does not equal accuracy; many sources can share the same mistake.
wrong.3: People on forums share opinions, not verified facts.
